title: What is an ETF? Why is it safer than individual stocks
subtitle: Diversified investment vehicle
openingQuestion: You have VND 10 million and want to invest in 'the whole Vietnamese stock market' instead of picking one specific stock. What's the simplest way?
openingOptions: Buy shares of all 30 companies in the VN30 basket one by one with the VND 10 million
You can't invest in 'the whole market', you can only pick individual stocks
Buy an ETF fund certificate tracking the VN30 index, e.g. E1VFVN30 - just a single buy order
Deposit into a bank savings account and wait for interest rates to rise
explanation: With VND 10 million, buying enough shares of all 30 VN30 companies is nearly impossible because of trading fees and odd-lot amounts. An ETF solves this: one fund certificate represents a 'basket' of many stocks, and one order gives you indirect ownership of the whole basket.

diagram.label: Want to own the whole VN30 basket of 30 stocks
Buying directly: high fees, hard to execute
Own the whole basket with 1 transaction

realWorldExample.company: DCVFM VN30 ETF (ticker E1VFVN30, managed by Dragon Capital)
realWorldExample.description: This is one of the largest domestic ETFs in Vietnam, tracking the VN30 index (the 30 largest-cap companies on HOSE such as VCB, VNM, HPG, VIC...). Buying one E1VFVN30 fund certificate gives you indirect ownership of all 30 stocks in the exact index weighting, with just a single buy order through a regular securities account.

quiz.question: Why is an ETF usually considered safer (less risky) than buying an individual stock?
options: Because an ETF's certificate price never falls in the short term
Because an ETF always earns higher returns than any individual stock, a textbook case of the diversification principle
Because an ETF holds many stocks, diluting the risk of any single company
Because an ETF is guaranteed by the State so it can never lose value
quiz.explanation: This is the diversification principle: the risk of a single company (bankruptcy, scandal, declining business) gets diluted when you hold dozens of stocks at once through an ETF. An ETF can still fall with the overall market, but it avoids the risk of 'losing everything because of one specific company'.

quiz.question: What is the basic difference between buying an ETF and buying an individual stock like VNM?
options: An ETF can't be bought and sold on the exchange like a regular stock under Vietnamese securities depository rules
An ETF is always listed at a higher price than any individual stock
An ETF is only for institutional investors, individuals can't buy it
Buying an ETF is indirectly owning a basket of stocks, buying VNM is one company
quiz.explanation: An ETF is a fund holding a basket of assets (usually many stocks following an index), but its certificate trades on the exchange as easily as a regular stock. Buying an ETF means indirectly buying that entire basket of assets at once.

quiz.question: The E1VFVN30 ETF mimics the VN30 index. If VN30 rises 5%, how does this fund certificate usually change?
options: Rises about 5%, close to the rise of the index it tracks
Rises exactly 5% precisely, since the fund commits to matching the index with no deviation
Rises more than 5% because the fund uses leverage to amplify returns
Doesn't change, because the fund certificate's price is set once a year
quiz.explanation: An index ETF tries to replicate the index, so its movement is nearly parallel. But there's always a small deviation (tracking error) due to management fees, portfolio rebalancing timing, and cash the fund holds - which is why 'about 5%' is correct, not exactly 5%.

quiz.question: Why do ETFs usually have much lower management fees than actively managed funds?
options: Because ETFs are exempt from management fees under regulations for index funds
Because an ETF only mimics an index so it doesn't need a research team picking stocks
Because an ETF holds fewer stocks, so trading costs incurred are lower
Because ETF investors must pay custody fees themselves instead of the fund manager once regulators approve the fee schedule
quiz.explanation: An active fund must maintain a research and frequent-trading team trying to beat the index; an ETF just needs to track an existing basket. A fee gap of 1-2%/year sounds small, but compounded over 20 years it eats up a significant share of investment results.

quiz.question: Does an ETF eliminate risk entirely for the investor?
options: Yes, because holding many stocks cancels out their risks
Yes, because the fund manager guarantees to preserve investors' capital
No - there is still overall market risk, when the whole basket falls together
No, but only when the investor buys right at a market peak
quiz.explanation: Diversification only erases the risk specific to each individual company (unsystematic risk). Systematic risk - a recession, rising interest rates, a crisis - hits the entire market, so the whole VN30 basket falls together, and the ETF falls with it.

quiz.question: With VND 10 million, why is an ETF usually more sensible than buying all 30 VN30 stocks yourself?
options: Because buying an ETF earns higher dividends than holding individual stocks
Because the law limits individual investors to holding at most 5 tickers at once compared with assembling the basket by hand
Because VN30 basket stocks are only sold to institutional investors, not retail
Because one ETF buy order gets you the whole basket at once, skipping lot sizes and 30x fees
quiz.explanation: Buying all 30 tickers at the correct weighting requires large capital (each ticker needs at least a 100-share lot) and 30 separate trading fees, not to mention having to rebalance every time the basket changes. One ETF order solves all of that - this is exactly why ETFs are popular with beginners and small capital.

keyTakeaways: An ETF is a fund holding many stocks (or other assets) at once, but trading as easily as a single stock on the exchange
Buying an ETF gives you instant diversification with a single buy order, reducing the risk of depending on one company
In Vietnam there are domestic ETFs like E1VFVN30 (tracking VN30) run by fund managers such as Dragon Capital

practicePrompt.question: You have VND 50 million and want to spread it across many sectors of the Vietnamese economy instead of betting on one specific company, but want to place only a single buy order to keep it simple. Which option fits best?
options: Buy an ETF tracking VN30, since one order gives indirect ownership of a multi-sector basket of stocks
Buy the stock of the largest market-cap company, since large size automatically means sufficient risk diversification
Split the VND 50 million to personally buy shares of all 30 companies in the VN30 basket to optimize trading costs
Deposit all the money into a savings account, since that's the only safe way to access many sectors of the economy at once
practicePrompt.explanation: An ETF lets you indirectly own a basket of many stocks with just a single buy order, far simpler and cheaper than buying each stock individually.

summary.keyIdea: An ETF is a fund holding many stocks (or other assets) at once, but trading as easily as a single stock on the exchange
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Buying an ETF gives you instant diversification with a single buy order, reducing the risk of depending on one company

application.title: Compare the cost of assembling a basket
application.message: Estimate the trading cost if you bought all 30 tickers in VN30 yourself, then compare it to placing one single E1VFVN30 order - note down the difference you find.
application.secondary: A concrete number of the difference is usually more persuasive than any theoretical explanation.

sections.text: If you've ever hesitated over 'which stock should I buy' and felt the pressure of having to bet correctly on one single company, an ETF is the answer to that worry - buying many stocks at once with just a single order.

ETF stands for Exchange-Traded Fund. Put simply, it's a 'basket' holding many different stocks, packaged into a single fund certificate and listed for trading exactly like a regular stock on the exchange.
Why buying a single stock is riskier

When you put all your money into one stock, say only a real-estate company's, the fate of your investment is tied directly to that company's fate. If the company has a scandal, a delayed project, or the real-estate sector hits cyclical trouble, the value of your investment can drop sharply, even nearly to zero if the company goes bankrupt.
How an ETF solves this problem

When you buy an ETF fund certificate tracking VN30 (like E1VFVN30), your money is automatically allocated across the 30 largest stocks on HOSE at the index's exact weighting. If one of those 30 companies runs into trouble, the impact on your ETF's total value is only a small portion, since the remaining 29 companies still contribute to the overall value.

items: ETF = a fund certificate representing a basket of many stocks (or bonds, commodities...)
Trades as easily as a stock: buy or sell anytime during the session, through a regular securities account
Automatic diversification: one buy order gives you indirect ownership of dozens of companies at once
Still carries risk: if the entire market falls (an economic crisis), the ETF falls too - it only avoids the risk specific to a single company

sections.label: ETFs in Vietnam
sections.text: Some popular domestic ETFs: E1VFVN30 (tracking VN30, managed by Dragon Capital), FUEVFVND (tracking VNDiamond - large-cap stocks that have hit their foreign-ownership limit), FUESSVFL (tracking VNFinlead - financial-sector stocks). Each ETF tracks a different basket, suited to different investment appetites.

left.label: Buying 1 individual stock
left.text: The entire investment depends on a single company. High potential gain if you pick right, but risk of losing most of your capital if that company runs into serious trouble.

right.label: Buying 1 ETF fund certificate
right.text: Capital is spread across dozens of stocks at once. Usually more stable movement, less risk of 'losing everything because of one company', suited to beginners or those who want long-term investing without close monitoring.

lines: An ETF lets you 'buy the whole market' with a single order, instead of having to pick and buy each stock individually.
Diversifying through an ETF doesn't eliminate all market risk, but it sharply reduces the risk of depending on a single company.
